scenes.text: In South Africa, a patient's medical history doesn't live in one place. It's scattered — across paper folders, provincial hospital systems, laboratory databases, medical aid claims, and private hospital records. To understand how a doctor pieces it together, let's follow one patient's data, from the moment it's created.

First, the landscape. About sixty-two million people live in South Africa. Roughly nine million of them are covered by a medical scheme. Everyone else — around five in six people — depends mainly on the public health system. And these two sectors run on almost entirely separate infrastructure.

Our patient — a hypothetical woman we'll call Nomsa — walks into a public clinic. At reception, she's registered on the Health Patient Registration System, or H P R S: a national, online registry built for National Health Insurance. It looks her up by her ID number, and issues her a patient registration number.

But H P R S records who she is — not what's wrong with her. Her clinical story — symptoms, blood pressure, diagnosis, treatment — is written by hand, in a paper folder, filed at this clinic. In most public clinics, that folder is still the clinical record. A national electronic medical record did go live in March 2025 — as a beta, in thirty-six clinics and one GP practice.

Her visit is also counted. Staff tick it off in a paper register. At the end of the month, the ticks are totalled onto a form, and captured into D H I S 2 — the District Health Information System. D H I S 2 stores totals: how many visits, how many tests. It holds no names. It tells the health department what's happening — not what happened to Nomsa.

Now suppose Nomsa tests positive for HIV, and starts treatment. Her details enter another system: TIER dot Net, the national register for antiretroviral therapy. A data capturer reads her paper folder, and types the information in. Depending on its size, a clinic keeps this register on paper, on a standalone computer, or on a networked system.

Her blood is sent to the National Health Laboratory Service, which runs more than a hundred and ten million tests a year. The sample is logged in its laboratory system, TrakCare Lab. The result comes back to the clinic through a web viewer — or, for some HIV and TB tests, a small SMS printer on the clinic wall. A nurse writes the result into the paper folder. A data capturer copies it into TIER dot Net.

Once she's stable, her chronic medicine can be packed centrally and collected near home, through a programme called C C M D D — at a private pharmacy, a GP, or a community pick-up point. Separately, the Stock Visibility System tracks whether clinics have medicines on the shelf. It follows boxes — not patients.

Months later, Nomsa is referred to a hospital. What travels with her is a referral letter — on paper. What the hospital runs depends on the province. In an August 2025 reply to Parliament, the Health Department listed them. The Western Cape runs Clinicom, in fifty-three hospitals. The Eastern Cape, HMS2, in forty-four. The Free State, HMS2 and Meditech. KwaZulu-Natal, its own eHealth system, in forty-two hospitals. Gauteng, a SAP-based Health Information System. And in Mpumalanga, North West, Limpopo and the Northern Cape — no patient information or electronic record system at hospitals.

The Western Cape goes further. Its Provincial Health Data Centre links clinic visits, admissions, lab results, pharmacy records and HIV registers to a single patient number — covering around eight million people. Clinicians can view it through a web tool called the Single Patient Viewer. It's the closest thing the public sector has to one joined-up record. And it stops at the provincial border.

Say instead that Nomsa arrives by ambulance. Paramedics document her care on a patient report form — in many services, still on paper. At the emergency department, they hand her over out loud, in a structured format, and leave the form behind. If she needs blood, it comes from the South African National Blood Service — or in the Western Cape, the Western Cape Blood Service — each with its own computer system. Her X-rays are stored in a digital image archive, called a PACS — standard in private radiology, far patchier in public hospitals.

Now, the private side. Suppose Nomsa gets a job with medical aid, and sees a private GP. The practice runs practice-management software — products like GoodX, or Healthbridge. These are built around billing. They store her notes — but only on that practice's system.

Every consultation creates a claim. It travels through a switching house, such as Healthbridge or MediKredit, in a standard electronic format called PHISC MEDCLM — carrying tariff codes and ICD-10 diagnosis codes — to her scheme, often in real time. The scheme now knows what she was treated for, and what was paid. That's billing data, not a clinical record. But it's often the most complete history of her private care that exists anywhere.

Her GP sends blood to a private laboratory — Ampath, Lancet, or PathCare. The result goes back to the doctor who asked for it, through that lab's own portal or app. Her prescription is filled at a retail pharmacy, whose dispensing software — ProPharm, for example — sends its own claim through a switch.

If she's admitted to a private hospital, she enters that group's system. Netcare's electronic record, CareOn, runs across forty-five of its hospitals — on more than thirteen thousand iPads, with about thirty-one thousand users. But CareOn serves Netcare. Mediclinic and Life Healthcare run their own systems. And the specialists who treat her are mostly independent practices — with their own software again.

So: a new doctor sees Nomsa. How do they learn her history? First, they ask her. Then they read what she's carrying: a referral letter, a clinic card, her maternity case record, her child's Road to Health booklet — paper records that the patient holds, by design. If they have access, they look up results on a lab portal. If she was treated inside the same hospital group, or the same province, they may open its system. If she's a Discovery member and consents, the doctor can view a history built from claims and lab results, through HealthID. Anything else means a phone call, an email, or a fax to another facility — and a signed request for copies of her records.

The rules allow this. The Protection of Personal Information Act permits health professionals to process health information to treat a patient. Standards exist too: a national interoperability framework, first published in 2014, points to international standards such as HL7. H P R S is meant to become the national master patient index. And the National Health Insurance Act, signed in May 2024, envisions a single national health information system — but it has not yet come into effect.
That's how the system works. Here's where it breaks.

First: there's no shared record. No national system lets a doctor pull a patient's history across provinces, or between public and private care. The information exists. It just isn't where the doctor is.

Second: identity. H P R S holds more than sixty-eight million patient records — more than the country's population. Only about thirty-two and a half million have been verified against Home Affairs. Duplicate registrations can turn one person into several patients — and split one history in two.

Third: copying by hand. Results move from printer to folder, and folder to TIER dot Net, retyped each time. Every copy is a chance for error. Studies of TIER dot Net have found patient outcomes misreported.
Fourth: paper. A folder filed at one clinic can't be read at another. It can be lost, misfiled, or simply not there when the patient is.
Fifth: the provincial patchwork. Different hospital systems in different provinces — and in four provinces, no hospital patient system at all.
Sixth: the data that does move is often the wrong kind. D H I S 2 moves counts, not patients. Claims move codes and costs — not results, or notes.

And finally, the wall between sectors. Public systems, private hospital groups, labs and medical schemes each hold a piece. For a patient who moves between them — as millions do — no single doctor sees the whole picture.
The data exists. It's created every day, at every visit. It just doesn't travel with the patient.
